1:
The flies are contested. Delitzsch argues that the Hebrew phrase means deadly flies rather than dead ones, since the genitive construction matches expressions like instruments of death, whereas using it for a plain adjective would be an affected poeticism without parallel; he mentions a proposal to read dung-flies, and the possibility that what is meant is flies carrying death from corpses to the living, noting how finely the Assyrian lists distinguish varieties of fly. He concedes the objection that any fly falling into the pot would spoil it. Gill keeps both senses open, reporting an old reading in which the flies are winter-weakened insects that die in the ointment, and another in which they carry something poisonous by nature. Clarke generalises: any putrefaction spoils perfume.

What the image is for is not in dispute. Henry explains why a small fault costs a reputation so much more than the same fault in an obscure man: envy fastens on eminence and makes the worst of the lapses of those already cried up for wisdom, so that what would pass unnoticed elsewhere is severely censured. Anyone who professes religion must therefore walk circumspectly, many eyes being on the watch for his halting. Clarke puts the same warning as a lament — how many have tarnished in one unguarded moment what they spent years acquiring — and adds that no one can be called safe until he is in paradise.

On the hands the commentators agree and then diverge in emphasis. Gill sets aside the anatomical question, observing that the heart sits in the same place in both men, and makes the point one of readiness: the wise man's understanding is at hand when he needs it, and inclines him toward the things above. Clarke works the physical fact, that the right hand is the stronger and better exercised, and takes the pair as figures for the command a wise man keeps over his mind and the fool's want of any guard on his passions or his tongue. Wesley notes only that the right hand is the common instrument of action. Ellicott prefers a slightly different construction, that wisdom leads a man toward his right hand, and draws from it the book's recurring concession: the results of wisdom often disappoint, but its superiority to folly is not in doubt.

The third verse turns on one pronoun. The Latin and others took the fool to be calling everybody else a fool, and Ellicott records that reading before rejecting it as less obvious than the sense in which he betrays himself. Delitzsch, who treats these verses as a single quatrain, notes that the word order pushes on the way into prominence, because the fool is now being watched in public; and he corrects a rendering that would have the man lacking a heart altogether, when the Hebrew says his understanding fails him. Clarke and Henry both take the self-betrayal for granted and press it: in any company the man shows what he is, cannot conceal it, and is not ashamed of it.
4:
Leave not thy place is read three ways. Delitzsch takes it literally of an office: the man addressed is a subordinate official, told not to abandon the post he was given. He rejects Luther's attempt to tie the verse to the fool of the previous line, ruler and fool being different men, and denies that the clause means keeping one's composure. Clarke reads it as humility — that is thy place and duty — extending the counsel to a child before a parent and any inferior before a superior. He then reports, without endorsing, a patristic reading in which the ruler is Satan and the advice is not to despair of mercy, adding that this is true whether or not it is in the text. Ellicott shifts the second clause: the Hebrew word is healing, and what is quieted may be less the ruler's displeasure than the offences the subject would otherwise commit. Henry supplies the situation, a prosperous and over-taxed people growing insolent, and advises against throwing up a commission in a passion, princes being seldom implacable.

The error proceeding from a ruler is agreed to be misplaced promotion; the interest lies in who is displaced. Delitzsch insists the rich of the second clause are the nobly born, whose inheritance gives a claim to station and the means of training for it, and that the great heights are of the highest degree rather than a number of posts. Wesley makes them wealthy in endowments of mind. Henry has it both ways: men of shattered brains and broken fortunes preferred, while men of good sense and good estates, whose wealth would put them above bribery, sit low — unvalued, or unwilling to meet the terms. Clarke calls it favouritism that has ruined prosperous nations, naming two English chancellors; Gill names two biblical courtiers instead. On the horses, Gill notes that mounts were scarce in Judea and reserved for princes, so a servant riding was unseemly and a sign he had risen on his master's ruin; Ellicott turns the fact into a date, a noble ashamed to walk implying an age later than Solomon's.

The four hazards divide the commentators more sharply than anything else here, because they disagree whether these proverbs continue the political argument. Ellicott says plainly that no one has traced the connection successfully, that the theme is simply the advantage of caution in large undertakings, and that it forces the sense to make the undertaking a rebellion. Henry does exactly that, at length: the digger of the pit is prince or subject alike, whose violence returns on his own head; the hedge is the fence God drew round a ruler's prerogative, so a conspirator twists his own halter; the stones are pulled down by a reformer who finds it easier to demolish good than build better; the knotty timber is a people that will not split by force. Delitzsch takes the pressure off all four by observing that the verbs express possibility, not certainty, since as predictions they would be false to experience.

Smaller points survive. Delitzsch and Ellicott both identify the hedge as a dry stone wall of the kind snakes nest in, and Ellicott notices that the Hebrew for breaking it down inverts a prophet's phrase about repairing the breach, and that the word for pit occurs nowhere else in the Old Testament. Clarke records a proposal that the biter is a thorn, not a serpent, its prick being like a sting. On the blunt iron Ellicott confesses the verse very obscure and keeps the received rendering for want of better, the word for edge being literally face. Gill applies the removal of stones to those who shift the landmarks of commonwealths, Wesley to men attempting what is too heavy for them. Henry and Clarke agree on the moral: whet the tool instead of forcing it, since the mower loses no time sharpening his scythe.
11:
Who is the master of the tongue? Ellicott and Delitzsch both take the verse for a charmer who comes too late: if the snake has already struck for want of enchantment, his skill is worth nothing. Ellicott, who calls the verse difficult, follows the Greek there, notes how often eastern travellers describe the whispering of charmers, and suggests the illustration was chosen because the phrase master of the tongue leads into the verses on speech. Delitzsch records two rival constructions: a Talmudic reading making the opening word a question, so the serpent bites only under providential impulse, and a rabbinic fable in which the beasts ask what pleasure it takes in biting and are told the slanderer gains nothing either — there the master of the tongue is the calumniator, as the Targum, Jerome and Luther took it. Clarke and Gill take the second half as the point: the phrase means without hissing, and a snake may bite before it warns, as a slanderer injures by innuendo before saying anything plain. Henry adds that contradiction makes such a tongue more violent, so it must be charmed rather than out-talked.

The wise man's gracious words are read for their effect. Delitzsch has them gracious in substance, form and delivery, and therefore effective in winning favour, since cultivation earns goodwill. Wesley says the same in six words. Gill turns the noun into doctrine, so a gracious man's discourse runs on the grace of God; Clarke keeps it social, everything from such a man being decent and creditable. Against that stands the fool, whose lips swallow him. Delitzsch presses the verb, used elsewhere of gulping down or squandering and here of destruction, and charts the next verse's movement from mere absurdity to a madness compounded of presumption, wantonness and frenzy. Henry supplies a political mechanism — seditious talk brings a man to official notice — and cites a prince whose request cost him his life. No wonder, he adds, that men who begin foolishly end madly, an ungoverned tongue growing more violent the more liberty it has.

On the fool's abundance of words the commentators grow cheerful. Gill describes him repeating himself, saying whatever comes uppermost, holding forth on every subject whether he knows it or not, and engrossing the conversation though the least fit of the company for it. Henry observes that what is wanting in weight he supplies in number, and states the rule that many empty of sense are full of words, the least solid being the noisiest; he offers the second clause either as a rebuke to boasting, since nobody knows what a day will bring, or as mockery of the man's tautology. Delitzsch takes the clause as a subordinate concession — the fool talks on although nobody knows the future — and reports that the ancient versions tried to smooth away its repetition. Ellicott would introduce it with and yet, setting the fool's volubility against the cautious silence experience teaches a wise man.

The closing verse is grammatically awkward and proverbially plain. Delitzsch works the difficulties, a plural subject resolving into a distributive singular and a masculine noun construed as feminine, which he calls the greater anomaly, and rejects an old attempt to solve it by supplying a word. Clarke and Ellicott agree the second clause is a saying: the man cannot find the road to the next town, or his way along a plain road. Henry gets two things from the weariness. Some labour is absurd in itself, spent on food that perishes, and men choose that drudgery over liberty; other labour is good but made exhausting by being gone about awkwardly, which is why the duties of religion are complained of by those who bring no prudence to them. His closing turn is the best line here: the road to the heavenly city is a highway on which wayfaring men, though fools, do not go wrong.
16:
The child king is not merely a minor. Gill lists young princes under whom nations prospered, and defines the fault as childishness of understanding — a ruler who minds his pleasures as children mind their play, fickle, self-willed, unwilling to be advised. Henry adds that the body staggers when the head is giddy, guessing that Solomon wrote foreseeing the son who stayed a child all his life. Clarke argues from politics: regencies breed civil war or oppression, and a prince raised under interested tutors rules partially once of age. Ellicott notes that the Hebrew word ranges from lad to servant, and that some read servant here to sharpen the contrast with the nobly born king. Delitzsch allows servant but not slave, and so rejects an attempt to date the book by making the verse a hit at Herod.

The blessing that follows is read for legitimacy or for character. Clarke wants both: the Greek renders it son of freemen, men bred to the principles of civil liberty, and an incontestable hereditary right takes long to establish, so a state without one lies open to pretenders. Gill derives the Hebrew word from whiteness, of the robes such men wore or of their manners, and insists the point is imitation rather than descent, since illustrious families produce ignoble administrations. Wesley settles it in a line: nobles not by birth so much as by disposition. Henry's rule on the eating is that magistrates eat for strength, so their bodies may serve their souls in the service of God and their country, not for drunkenness, which unfits a man to judge. Wesley marks the morning as the time for weighty affairs.

Whether the last three verses continue the mirror for princes divides them. Ellicott takes them for isolated proverbs and thinks the plain English sense right, reporting how those who trace continuity read them: decay, riot, and a warning against rebellion. Delitzsch does trace it, holding that the proverb on sloth gains force here and that the indefinite subject of the feast means the princely men just described. Henry lets the figure run: the neglected roof lets in rain, the timber rots, and so it goes with a family behind on its business and a state whose treasure is spent. On the dual form of the word for idleness the two divide: Gill allows it to mean both hands, or body and mind, or every rank of person, while Delitzsch denies that Hebrew forms attributive duals and takes it as intensive, a doubled and constant laziness. Clarke reduces the whole to a saying about a stitch in time.

Money answering all things is where Henry is most careful. A feast is made for conversation as much as food, he says, and wine gladdens life, but money procures the house, the bed, the clothing and the children's portions — and yet of itself answers nothing, since it neither feeds nor clothes, and as an instrument of exchange reaches no further than this life, buying neither pardon nor peace of conscience. Clarke lets two passages of Horace make the point, on men born only to consume the produce of the soil and on money as the queen who bestows friends, honour and beauty. Gill identifies the feast-makers as the princes already described. The chapter closes on secrecy. Delitzsch observes that the Greek rendered the word for thought as conscience, which is not quite its meaning though it touches it, naming the inner awareness that judges by moral standards; he rejects a proposal to make it a study-chamber. Ellicott notes that the word belongs to later Hebrew, and that the winged creature is literally a master of wings. Clarke wonders whether carrier pigeons are meant, and reproduces a Targum in which Elijah flies about publishing what men say in private. Henry keeps it plain: sin begins in the mind, so the first risings must be checked.
